sections.label: Article 98 Judge tenure
sections.summary: Article 98 protects Supreme Court Judges' tenure to age 65 and bars disadvantageous changes to appointment terms.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Under our Constitution, Article 98 protects the security of tenure of Supreme Court Judges till the age of 65 years.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: Article 98 provides, among other things, that the office of a Supreme Court Judge must not be abolished during the Judges' continuance in office and that the terms of appointment, including remuneration, shall not be altered to the Judges' disadvantage after his appointment.

sections.label: Retirement age since 1969
sections.summary: The retirement age of 65 was introduced in 1969, when Singapore's life expectancy was 67.6 years.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: The current retirement age of 65 years was introduced way back in 1969, more than half a century ago, when the life expectancy in Singapore was 67.6 years.

sections.label: UK Judge retirement age
sections.summary: The UK recently raised its Judges' retirement age from 70 to 75 to retain their invaluable experience.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
sentences.text: In the United Kingdom (UK), the age of retirement for Judges was recently increased from 70 to 75 years, just two years ago, with the reason cited that raising the retirement age would mean that the Judges' invaluable experience could be retained.

sections.label: Judges' average Bench years
sections.summary: Most Judges spend an average of about 15 years on the Bench by the time they reach 65.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: From the time of appointment to the time a Judge reaches the age of 65, most Judges would have spent an average of about 15 years on the Bench.

sections.label: Retirement age balance factors
sections.summary: The retirement age of 65 and re-appointment framework balance factors including younger Judges' advancement, retaining older Judges' experience, and Bench composition.

sentences.speaker: The Second Minister for Law (Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai)
sentences.text: Apart from this, the retirement age of 65 – as well as the framework for re-appointment, or the appointment of Senior Judges – allows us to strike a good balance between various factors at play here, including providing younger Judges with the opportunity to advance, whilst retaining the experience of the older generation; and also allowing for calibrations to be made to the composition of the Bench from time to time, in consideration of whether the Bench has the right mix of different skillsets in various different legal disciplines, to meet the evolving justice needs of society.

sections.label: Chief Justice extension remarks
sections.summary: The Chief Justice said in a November speech that a Judge approaching 65 would ordinarily be offered an extension to 68.

sentences.speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
sentences.text: Minister, last November, the Chief Justice revealed in a speech he made at the Supreme Court that when a Judge approached 65 years of age, he would ordinarily be offered an extension to continue in office till the age of 68.

sections.label: Judge retirement extension age
sections.summary: The Chief Justice says a Judge reaching 65 is ordinarily offered an extension up to 68.

sentences.speaker: Mr Edwin Tong Chun Fai
sentences.text: On Ms Lim's first point, the Chief Justice says that when a Judge reaches 65, he is ordinarily offered an extension up to 68.
